turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, I guess... well, they brought me in. I didn't really want to come, but my boss kind of made it a whole thing. It's because of what's been happening at the warehouse. I work freight, moving stock and materials around—I've been doing it since I took a break from my college classes—and it's a huge place, really loud, lots of moving parts. But I guess they brought me in because I keep doing things there that they don't understand. 

Like, I'll be standing by the forklift, right? And I just... I freeze. I'll freeze completely with my arms straight up in the air, just stuck like that right next to the machine. And I start copying the sounds it makes, like the backing-up warning sounds, I just keep making those exact beeping sounds out loud, over and over, and doing the hand signals that the spotters use to guide the trucks. And with the freight itself, the actual boxes, I can't just stack them normally on the pallets. I keep moving them into these strange little patterns, like specific shapes and sequences on the concrete, shifting them around into these exact little designs. And the whole time, the foreman and everyone else on the floor are just yelling at me, they're screaming for me to stop and just load the trucks, but I just keep moving the boxes in the patterns and doing the hand signals and the beeps. So, yeah, they said I was acting too weird and I had to come see a doctor.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing in rigid postures, echoing sounds (echolalia), copying movements (echopraxia), and arranging boxes in strange, repetitive patterns despite being told to stop, which are clear indicators of disorganized and abnormal motor behavior.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been experiencing these behaviors, like the sounds and the repetitive movements, since you were a child, or is this something that only started recently?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, no, not since I was a kid. When I was little, I mean, I played with toys and stuff like any normal kid, building blocks and Legos and all that, but I never got stuck like I do now. I never froze up like a statue or made backing-up truck noises in the middle of the classroom, you know? I was just a regular kid. I even did fine in my college classes before I decided to take a break and work freight. So this is... this is definitely a newer thing. It really all started, I'd say, about six months ago. 

Yeah, roughly six months. I remember because it was right around the time they brought in this massive new shipment of inventory at the warehouse, and I just started noticing the way things absolutely needed to be arranged. For the last six months, it's been happening pretty much constantly. The strange behavior, the freezing up by the forklifts, making the beeping sounds... and it's not just the movements, either, it's the talking. People keep telling me my talking is confusing now. Like, I'll be trying to explain to the foreman why the boxes have to go in that specific shape on the concrete, how the sequence has to be exactly right for the space, and the words just... I guess they don't make sense to anyone else. They say I'm talking nonsense or that my sentences are all mixed up and confusing to listen to. But I'm just trying to explain the patterns to them! 

So between the confusing talking and all the strange behavior on the floor with the freight, it's been about half a year of this. Day in, day out, for six solid months. Every single shift, the same thing. It just takes over, you know? Like the hand signals, I have to do them, and the beeping, it just has to come out exactly like the machine. But yeah, definitely not since childhood. Just the last six months. I mean, if I did this my whole life, I wouldn't have even gotten hired at the warehouse in the first place, right? So it's just been these past six months that everything got so intense and they started making such a big deal out of it.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient reports that others find their speech confusing, nonsensical, and mixed up when they try to explain things.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing up like a statue, making repetitive beeping noises like a machine, and performing specific hand signals.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices talking to you, or see things that other people don't seem to notice?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? No, no, I don't hear anyone talking to me, except, you know, the foreman yelling at me to move the pallets, which is definitely real, unfortunately. I mean, it's a warehouse, right? So it's incredibly loud anyway. There is the constant hum of the overhead ventilation, the grinding of the pallet jacks, that heavy thud when a loaded pallet drops onto the concrete, the metal scraping on the floor... but no, no floating voices or people whispering in my ear or anything like that. 

And seeing things? No, I see exactly what is actually there. I mean, that is the whole point of what I am doing. I see the boxes, I see the sharp corners of the boxes, the corrugated cardboard, the way the edges have to line up perfectly. I see the exact space on the concrete floor where they absolutely have to go. Some of the guys on the floor ask me that sometimes, they ask if I am seeing ghosts or something out there in the aisles when I stop moving. But I am not. I am just looking at the inventory. The inventory is entirely real. The forklift is real. The beeping... well, the beeping I make is real, and the forklift backing up is real. 

I don't need to see things that aren't there because the things that are there are already so... so demanding, you know? They take up all my attention, just the pure geometry of it all, how the freight has to be stacked, the exact sequence of the shapes on the ground. If I was hearing voices, I wouldn't be able to concentrate on the hand signals for the spotters, right? Because you have to be extremely precise with the hand signals. You bring your arms straight up, you hold them there, you freeze... it requires total, absolute focus on the physical objects right in front of you, the machinery and the space. So no, no voices, no invisible things, just the freight, the machines, and the patterns.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes abnormal motor behaviors, including freezing in the aisles, holding their arms straight up and freezing (posturing/catalepsy), and making beeping noises (stereotypy/mannerism).
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a head injury, a seizure, or been told by a doctor that you have any medical problems involving your brain?
turns.patient_response:
A head injury? No, no, definitely not. I mean, working freight, you'd think maybe that could happen, right? Because there are heavy things everywhere, pallets stacked three, sometimes four levels high on the industrial racking, steel beams, the forks on the lifts swinging around... but they are actually really, really strict about safety on the floor. We have these bright yellow hard hats we have to wear in certain zones, the drop zones, and I always wear mine. I make sure it's strapped right, perfectly centered on my head, because if a corrugated box comes down, you absolutely want that protection. But no, nothing has ever hit me. I've never fallen and hit my head on the concrete, never been knocked out, never had a concussion. Not even when I was little and riding bikes or whatever. 

And a seizure? No, I've never had a seizure in my life. I know what those are, I know what they look like—where someone falls down and shakes, or maybe they just stare off into space and their brain kind of short-circuits and they don't remember anything that happened. But see, when I freeze up by the forklift, like I was telling you before? I am completely awake. I am totally aware. I remember every single second of it. I'm not having a seizure, I'm just holding the position because the position has to be held. I'm doing the hand signals. My brain is fully awake and processing the geometry of the space. 

And no doctor has ever told me I have a brain problem, either. Actually, I had to get a full medical physical before I started at the warehouse, you know, just to prove I could safely lift fifty pounds and stand on my feet for a full eight-hour shift. It was a whole process. The doctor checked my blood pressure, listened to my heart, he took this little light and made me track his pen back and forth with my eyes to check my pupils... and he signed off on all the paperwork right there in the office. He said I was in great shape. Perfectly healthy. So physically, medically, my brain is completely fine. No injuries, no seizures, no brain diseases or anything like that. Just a perfectly normal medical record.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing up and 'holding the position because the position has to be held,' which indicates posturing or catalepsy, a form of disorganized or abnormal motor behavior.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been feeling unusually energized, needing much less sleep than usual, or perhaps feeling extremely down or hopeless during these past six months?
turns.patient_response:
Energized? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, working freight is physically exhausting, just totally draining. You're on your feet for eight, sometimes ten hours if they call mandatory overtime, just constantly moving, bending, lifting, pulling the manual pallet jacks. By the time my shift ends and I clock out at the punch machine, I am completely wiped out. I go home, I take a hot shower because you get this thick layer of warehouse dust on you—it's like this fine, gray powder from the cardboard and the concrete that just settles on your skin and your clothes, you know? 

And then I go right to sleep. I definitely don't need less sleep. I need my full eight hours, sometimes nine, just to let my muscles recover from the lifting. I have this alarm clock, one of those loud digital ones, and when it goes off at 4:30 AM, I am dragging myself out of bed just like anyone else on the morning shift. So no, no crazy bursts of energy where I'm staying up all night or feeling like I don't need to rest. I mean, I'll drink a Monster energy drink in the breakroom sometimes, usually the green can, just to get through that afternoon slump around 2:00 PM, but everybody does that. That's just regular tired. 

And as for feeling extremely down or hopeless... no, not at all. I don't feel sad. I don't sit around crying or feeling like life is pointless, nothing like that. I actually feel like I have a very clear purpose right now, with the inventory and the patterns. It's just... it's a lot of responsibility, you know? Making sure the corrugated boxes are aligned perfectly on the concrete, making sure the forklift signals are exact and the geometry is respected. If anything, I just feel really, really focused. 

Sometimes I get frustrated, sure, but only when the foreman comes over and yells at me to hurry up, or when the other guys just carelessly drop a box and mess up the sequence I just laid out. That is incredibly frustrating because they just don't see the shapes, they don't see how the corners have to fit the space on the floor perfectly. But it's not depression. I'm not hopeless. It's just... it's just the work, and the patterns, and making sure I get my sleep so I can go back and do it all exactly right the next day. So no, my energy and my mood, they're just normal. I just go to work and sleep.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling sad or sitting around crying.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient denies feeling unusually energized or having crazy bursts of energy.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly states they do not need less sleep and require their full eight to nine hours.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient explicitly denies feeling hopeless or feeling like life is pointless.

turns.doctor_question: When you say your sentences are mixed up and people don't understand you, can you tell me exactly what happens to your thoughts when you try to speak?
turns.patient_response:
It's like... okay, so, it's like the tracks in my head just switch without me pulling the lever, you know? I'll be right there in the middle of a shift, totally focused on the geometry of the floor like I was telling you, and the supervisor will come over to my zone by the loading docks. Let's say he's at dock four, and he asks me a very simple question. He asks me which pallets are going on the outbound truck. I know the answer. I have the exact sequence of the corrugated boxes perfectly mapped out in my head.

So I start trying to explain it to him. I open my mouth, and I start talking about the load sheet, because we have these specific load sheets they print out in the front office, and you have to follow the barcodes exactly. But right as I'm explaining the load sheet, my words just... they just jump. Suddenly, instead of the barcodes, I'm talking about my old house. The one we lived in before I started taking those college classes, the one with the cracked concrete in the driveway. 

And I can't stop the sentence, it just keeps sliding forward. From the old house, I start talking about fishing. Like, actual fishing, the fishing poles and the way the water moves, and then from the fishing, my mouth is suddenly talking about church boxes. You know, the specific cardboard boxes they use for the donation drives at church? Which, I mean, I guess is kind of related to the boxes in the warehouse because they're both cardboard, but the dimensions are completely different and they don't hold nearly the same amount of weight. 

But I'm just standing there, saying all of this out loud to the supervisor, thinking I'm answering his question about the truck. And by the time I'm done, by the time I finally stop talking, he's just staring at me with this completely blank expression on his face. Nobody knows what I meant. I meant to tell him about the pallets for the truck, but all this other stuff just spilled out in one big, long chain, and the actual freight just gets completely lost somewhere between the fishing and the church boxes. It's incredibly frustrating because the inventory is right there in my head, but the words just won't stay in a straight line on the way out.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech jumping from one unrelated topic to another (load sheet to old house to fishing to church boxes) making them incomprehensible to others, which is a clear example of disorganized thinking and speech (derailment/loose associations).

turns.doctor_question: When you are repeating those beeping sounds or performing those hand signals, are you doing them because you feel like you are imitating someone else or something you just heard or saw, or is it purely coming from your own internal need to complete the pattern?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... I mean, it's kind of both, right? Because the sounds are already there in the air, and I'm just mirroring them. Like, they drive these big Crown stand-up reach trucks on the floor, and whenever they throw it in reverse, there's this very specific, high-pitched safety alarm. It goes off at this exact, steady rhythm. And when I hear it, or when I see the spotter in the yellow vest waving them back into the racking zone, I just... I start copying the beeping sounds. I make the sound with my own mouth, trying to match the pitch perfectly, and I copy the exact hand signals the spotter is making. 

I guess... I mean, I guess that's actually why they brought me in here to see you in the first place, if I'm being honest. Because at the warehouse, I just keep doing things like that. I'll be right in the middle of a shift, and I'll just end up freezing with my arms up by the forklift, completely locked in that position, copying the beeping sounds and the hand signals. And it's not just the lifts, it's the freight, too. I'll start moving the corrugated boxes in these strange little patterns on the floor, sliding them around so the corners align perfectly with the expansion joints in the concrete, because the geometry has to be right. 

And the whole time I'm doing this, the foreman and the other guys on the shift are just losing their minds. They're standing right there, yelling for me to stop. Just screaming over the noise of the warehouse, "Hey, what are you doing? Put that on the pallet! Stop standing there with your arms up!" But I can't just drop the boxes or put my arms down just because they're getting mad. I'm copying the sounds, I'm holding the signals, I'm moving the boxes in the patterns, and they're just yelling and yelling. It's like they don't understand that once the lift starts backing up and the spotter makes the motion, the echo of it has to happen. I have to do it. But they just see me frozen there or sliding a box three inches to the left, and they think I'm just messing around, which I'm absolutely not. It's actually very precise work.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient explicitly describes freezing in locked positions (posturing/catalepsy), mirroring sounds (echolalia), copying hand signals (echopraxia), and moving boxes in strange patterns (stereotypy) despite others yelling at them to stop.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes feeling compelled to arrange boxes so their corners align perfectly with the floor joints because 'the geometry has to be right' and feeling an internal drive that they 'have to do it'.

turns.doctor_question: When you are at home or during times when you aren't working in the warehouse, do you find it difficult to start basic tasks, like getting yourself dressed or preparing a meal?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, not at all. I don't have any trouble starting things like that. I mean, like I was telling you earlier, my alarm goes off at 4:30 AM, that really loud digital one with the bright red numbers, and I get right up. I have to. Because if you're even one minute late to the punch machine at the front of the warehouse, the foreman writes you up on a yellow slip, and three of those means you're suspended. So getting dressed is... it's just a necessary part of the sequence. 

I actually have all my clothes laid out the night before, right on the edge of my wooden dresser. I always put on my heavy work jeans first, the ones with the reinforced knees because of all the bending and kneeling you have to do with the pallets, and then my shirt, and then my socks—the thick wool ones, because the concrete floor gets really cold in the mornings. And then my steel-toe boots. They're these heavy Timberlands, and I have to lace them up very specifically. I pull the laces tight from the bottom eyelets all the way to the top and double-knot them, because if a lace comes undone while you're pulling a manual jack with two thousand pounds of dog food or whatever freight on it, you could trip and the whole load could roll right over your foot. So I definitely get dressed. I never just sit on the edge of the bed unable to do it. I have to be ready.

And as for preparing meals, I mean, I have to eat to keep my strength up for the lifting. I make breakfast every single morning before I leave the apartment. It's a very structured process. I take out the small non-stick pan, I turn the front-right burner on the electric stove exactly to the number five—right in the middle, so it doesn't burn but it cooks evenly—and I scramble exactly three eggs. I use this black silicone spatula to push the eggs from the outside rim of the pan toward the center, creating these little folds, making sure nothing sticks to the edges and messes up the pan. And while that's cooking, I put two pieces of wheat bread in the toaster and press the lever down. When it pops up, I put exactly one square pat of butter on each slice, right in the center so it melts outward. 

Then I eat it, I wash the pan immediately with hot water and a blue sponge, I put the pan back in the cabinet on the left side under the counter, and I head out the door. So, no, I don't sit around struggling to figure out how to make food or put my clothes on. I have my routine, and I execute it every single day, exactly the way it needs to be done. It's just part of the schedule, just like the warehouse.

symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient explicitly denies having any trouble initiating basic daily tasks like getting dressed or preparing meals, which rules out avolition.
